title: UEFI bootkit infected fully patched Windows machines. Is Microsoft to blame?
gist: A new UEFI bootkit, BlackX, discovered by Kaspersky, bypassed Secure Boot on fully patched Windows machines by exploiting the 2022 Baton Drop flaw (CVE-2022-21894). Microsoft's fixes require a manual step to revoke the 2011 signing certificate, and few administrators know to take it. The author argues Microsoft should be much more explicit about this risk.

insights.claim: Organizations infected by the BlackX bootkit had installed all of Microsoft's 2022, 2023 and 2024 patches, yet the malware still bypassed Secure Boot by exploiting the Baton Drop flaw, CVE-2022-21894.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Being fully patched did not mean being protected, a gap that affects enterprise risk assessment and endpoint-security demand.
insights.locator: Microsoft had already patched the vulnerability

insights.claim: Fear of making potentially millions of devices unbootable kept Microsoft from enforcing revocation of the 2011 certificate, leaving a state of 'purgatory' that allowed BlackX three years after BlackLotus.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Supporting a legacy installed base creates long-running security debt that attackers can exploit.
insights.quote: This state of purgatory has existed ever since and is what allowed BlackX to bypass Secure Boot three years after BlackLotus.

insights.claim: Kaspersky says it is extremely unusual for administrators to take extra steps after installing an update, and Microsoft's activation instructions are buried deep on its website and hard for an average IT administrator to notice.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: When security depends on a manual step, few adopt it, and that creates systematic exposure across enterprise fleets.
insights.quote: These instructions for activating the patch are buried deep on the Microsoft website

insights.claim: Microsoft's mitigations added the Windows UEFI CA 2023 certificate in May 2023 and in 2024 provided a way to add Windows Production PCA 2011 to Secure Boot's forbidden-signatures database, but they did not revoke trust automatically.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The certificate migration is still incomplete, so remediation work across the PC ecosystem continues.

insights.claim: Microsoft's Knowledge Base post from two weeks ago, which it points customers to, nowhere warns that the patches released so far do nothing to protect against Baton Drop attacks. The status for home Windows users is also unclear.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Unclear vendor guidance shifts security liability onto customers and may draw regulatory attention.

insights.claim: The author frames a balancing act: revoking the key before the new one is installed turns a machine into an 'expensive paperweight', but trusting the old certificate for four-plus years makes exploitation almost inevitable. The middle ground would be clearer warnings.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The tradeoff between backward compatibility and security is structural for platform vendors with huge installed bases.
insights.quote: Allow the old patch to be trusted for four years and counting, and successful exploitation is almost inevitable.

insights.claim: UEFI bootkits are valuable to attackers because they run early in the boot process, load malicious kernel drivers before defenses start, are hard to detect without specialized tools, and can survive an OS reinstall.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Firmware-level persistence drives demand for specialized boot-integrity and firmware-security tools.
insights.quote: they combine stealth, persistence, and extensive control over the OS
insights.locator: What makes BlackLotus and BlackX so

insights.claim: BlackLotus, in 2023, was the first publicly documented in-the-wild UEFI bootkit to bypass Secure Boot on fully updated Windows 11, turning such bootkits from a theoretical threat into a real one.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Firmware attacks are now proven in the wild rather than theoretical, which changes how security teams prioritize them.

insights.claim: Kaspersky believes BlackX's operators bet that few organizations knew to activate the Baton Drop patch manually, and so invested time in studying BlackLotus to build a copycat.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Attackers target known mitigation gaps that are poorly communicated, so similar copycats are likely.
insights.quote: we believe they decided to invest time in understanding how BlackLotus works and creating a copycat of this bootkit

insights.claim: Baton Drop also allows BitLocker encryption keys to be extracted under certain conditions, in addition to bypassing Secure Boot.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: The flaw also exposes data-at-rest protection, which raises the potential breach impact.
